q: Li Tien voluntarily moved his clan and retainers to Yeh. How many people did he move in total, and which Han-dynasty figure did Ts'ao Ts'ao tease him about?
reply:
**Conclusion:** Li Dian (Li Tien, 李典) moved **13,000-plus people** — that is, over 13,000 “mouths” of his retainers and clan — to Ye (Yeh, 邺). Cao Cao (Ts’ao Ts’ao) teased him by asking whether he was trying to imitate **Geng Chun (耿纯)**, an Eastern Han founding general.

**Evidence from the *Sanguozhi*:** In the *Wei Shu* biography of Li Dian (SGZ Wei 18), it says Li Dian had “宗族部曲三千馀家” — over 3,000 households of clan members and retainers — living at Chengshi, and he asked permission to move them to Wei commandery. Cao Cao laughed and said:

> “卿欲慕耿纯邪？”  
> “Are you wishing to emulate Geng Chun?”

Li Dian replied that he did not presume to imitate Geng Chun; he simply wanted to strengthen the capital region. The text then records:

> “遂徙部曲宗族万三千馀口居邺。”  
> “So he moved his retainers and clan, 13,000-plus persons, to Ye.”

So the total moved was **13,000-plus persons**, not 13,000 households. The Han-dynasty figure Cao Cao mentioned was **Geng Chun**.

q: P'ang Te killed Kuo Yüan with his own hand in the battle at P'ing-yang. According to P'ei Sung-chih's commentary, how was Kuo Yüan related to Chung Yao? And how did Chung Yao react when he saw the head — what did he say?
reply:
Conclusion: According to Pei Songzhi’s commentary, **Guo Yuan (Kuo Yüan 郭援)** was **Zhong Yao’s (Chung Yao 钟繇) 外甥 (waisheng)** — that is, the son of Zhong Yao’s sister, so Zhong Yao was his maternal uncle. When Zhong Yao saw Guo Yuan’s severed head, he **“恸哭” (tongku)** — wailed/wept bitterly.

Basis: In the *Sanguozhi*, Pang De’s biography says Pang De personally cut off Guo Yuan’s head at Pingyang. Pei Songzhi’s note, citing *Fu Zi*, says:

> “援，钟繇之甥也。繇见援首，恸哭。太祖曰：‘援虽吾所恶，然繇为之恸哭，吾亦不忍。’”

Translation: “Guo Yuan was Zhong Yao’s nephew by his sister. When Zhong Yao saw Yuan’s head, he wept bitterly. Cao Cao said: ‘Yuan was someone I hated, but since Zhong Yao weeps bitterly for him, I too cannot bear it.’”

So the commentary does **not** record any words spoken by Zhong Yao himself; it records only that he wept. The quoted speech is Cao Cao’s.

q: How old was Lü Tai when he died, and in which year did he die?
reply:
I take “Lü Tai” to mean **Lü Dai (吕岱)**, the Wu general. In pinyin his name is **Lü Dai**; “Lü Tai” is a Wade-Giles-style rendering of the same name.

**Conclusion:** According to the *Sanguozhi*, Lü Dai died in **256 CE** at the recorded age of **96 sui** (Chinese age reckoning; roughly 95 by modern Western counting).

**Evidence:** In *Sanguozhi*, *Wu Shu* 15, the biography of Lü Dai says:  
> “太平元年，年九十六卒。”  
> “In the first year of Taiping, he died at age 96.”

“Taiping 1” corresponds to **256 CE**, during the reign of Sun Liang.

The *Sanguozhi* does not give a different age or year for him in Pei Songzhi’s annotations, as far as the standard record goes. The *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* does not focus on this detail; the age/year comes from the official history.

If you meant a different person named **Lü Tai (吕泰)**, I do not find a clear Three Kingdoms figure of that exact name in the *Sanguozhi* with a recorded death age and year.

q: When Liu Pei marched south from Chia-meng against Liu Chang, he left Huo Chün to hold the city. How long did Liu Chang's forces besiege it? How many soldiers did Huo Chün have, and how was the siege finally broken?
reply:
**Conclusion:** According to Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi* (Huo Jun’s biography), Liu Zhang’s forces besieged Jiameng for about/nearly a year. Huo Jun had only several hundred soldiers. The siege was broken by Huo Jun himself: when the besiegers grew lax, he selected elite troops, made a sudden sortie, routed them, and beheaded Xiang Cun.

**Evidence:** In the *Sanguozhi*, *Shu Shu*, “Huo Jun zhuan”:

> 先主自葭萌南还袭刘璋，留峻守葭萌城……后璋将扶禁、向存等帅万余人由阆水上，攻围峻，且一年，不能下。峻城中兵才数百人，伺其怠隙，选精锐出击，大破之，即斩存首。

Translation/points:
- Liu Bei marched south from **Jiameng** against **Liu Zhang**, leaving **Huo Jun** to hold Jiameng.
- Liu Zhang’s generals **Fu Jin** and **Xiang Cun** came with **over 10,000** men and besieged Huo Jun.
- The siege lasted **“且一年”** — “about/nearly a year.” The text does not give a precise month count.
- Huo Jun’s garrison was **“才数百人”** — only several hundred. The *Sanguozhi* does not specify an exact number.
- The siege was finally broken when Huo Jun waited for the enemy’s slack moment, chose his best troops, attacked out of the city, heavily defeated them, and cut off **Xiang Cun’s** head.

If your question comes from the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, the novel may give a rounder number such as “five hundred” for Huo Jun’s troops; the *Sanguozhi* wording is only **“several hundred.”** The basic outcome—Huo Jun holding out and then breaking the siege by a sortie—agrees with the historical account.

q: At Sun Hao's banquets, what was the minimum amount of wine every guest had to drink? Wei Yao could barely hold his liquor — how did Sun Hao accommodate him in the early days?
reply:
**Conclusion:** At Sun Hao’s banquets, the set quota was generally **seven *sheng*** of wine for every guest, able or not. Wei Yao (韦曜, also written Wei Zhao 韦昭) normally could not drink more than **two *sheng***. In the early period, while Sun Hao still treated him with special favor, he accommodated Wei Yao by **reducing his quota** or **secretly giving him tea to substitute for wine**. Later, when favor faded, Sun Hao forced him to drink and used it against him.

**Evidence:** This comes from the *Sanguozhi*, *Wu Shu*, *Sun Hao zhuan*, in Pei Songzhi’s commentary quoting the *Wu Lu*:

> “皓每飨宴，无不竟日，坐席无能否率以七升为限，虽不悉入口，皆浇灌取尽。曜素饮酒不过二升，初见礼异时，常为裁减，或密赐茶荈以当酒。至于宠衰，更见逼强，辄以为罪。”

Rough translation:

> “Every time Sun Hao held a banquet, it would invariably last the whole day. Among those seated, regardless of whether they could drink or not, the quota was generally seven *sheng*. Even if they did not drink it all, they were made to pour it down and finish it. Wei Yao by nature could not drink more than two *sheng*. When he was first treated with special courtesy, [Sun Hao] often reduced [his quota] for him, or secretly gave him tea to use as wine. But when favor declined, he was instead pressed hard and forced, and this was made a reason for punishment.”

So the minimum/quota was **seven *sheng***, and Wei Yao’s early accommodation was **reduced quota or secret tea substitution**. The exact modern equivalent of a *sheng* is uncertain, so I won’t convert it.

q: When I Chi went as an envoy to Wu, Sun Ch'üan deliberately asked him whether serving an unprincipled lord was tiring. How did I Chi reply?
reply:
According to Pei Songzhi’s commentary to the *Sanguozhi*, quoting the *Sanguo dianlüe*, Yi Ji (I Chi) replied:

**“一拜一起，未足为劳。”**  
**“One bow and one rising—not enough to be toil.”**

Sun Quan had asked him: **“劳事无道之君乎？”** — “Is it toilsome to serve an unprincipled lord?” Yi Ji was at that moment bowing to Sun Quan, so his answer cleverly turned the insult back on Sun Quan: merely bowing once and rising once was no labor. Sun Quan was impressed by his wit.

Note: this anecdote is preserved in **Pei Songzhi’s annotation**, not in Chen Shou’s main text.

q: When Han Ji was in charge of iron smelting, what did he replace the horse-driven bellows with? By how much did output improve?
reply:
**Conclusion:** Han Ji (韩暨, Hán Jì) replaced the horse-powered bellows (**马排**, mǎpái) with a **water-powered bellows (水排, shuǐpái)**, driven by a long/constant water current. The record says the benefit/output was **three times what it had been before** (“三倍于前”).

**Evidence:** In the *Sanguozhi* (*Wei Shu*, Han Ji’s biography), Chen Shou writes:

> “旧时冶作马排，每一熟石用马百匹；更作人排，又费功力；暨乃因长流为水排，计其利益，三倍于前。”

Rough translation: “Formerly, in smelting they used horse-powered bellows; for each smelting charge they used a hundred horses. They then made human-powered bellows, but that also wasted manpower. Han Ji therefore used a long-flowing stream to make water-powered bellows; calculating the benefit, it was three times as much as before.”

So: **horse-driven bellows → water-powered bellows; improvement: threefold.** The source does not give a precise modern output figure, only that the benefit was “three times” the previous level. This is from the official history, not a *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* story.

q: When Gao Rou submitted a memorial opposing the ban on commoners hunting deer, how many deer did he estimate the tigers in the imperial preserves were eating each year? How many tigers did he reckon the preserves held?
reply:
Gao Rou estimated that the predators in the imperial preserves were eating about **1,000 deer per year**, and he reckoned the preserves held **no more than 100** of them.

Basis: In the *Sanguozhi* (*Wei Shu*, “Gao Rou zhuan”), his memorial says:

> “今禁地之鹿，尽为虎狼所食。臣计虎狼所食，岁当千头。虎狼之数，不过百头。”

So: **1,000 deer/year**, **about 100 predators**.

One caveat: the Chinese text says **虎狼** (“tigers and wolves”), not only tigers. So if the question means strictly “tigers,” the original wording is broader; the number 100 is for the tigers-and-wolves in the preserves.

q: What was the original surname of He Qi's family? Why did they change it to He?
reply:
**Conclusion:** He Qi’s 贺齐 family originally had the surname **Qing 庆**. It was changed to **He 贺** in the Eastern Han because of a naming taboo: Emperor An of Han’s father, **Liu Qing 刘庆**, Prince of Qinghe 清河王, had the personal name **Qing 庆**, so the surname Qing was avoided and replaced by He.

**Evidence:** In the *Sanguozhi* 三国志, *Wu Shu* 吴书, *He Qi zhuan* 贺齐传, Pei Songzhi’s 裴松之 commentary quotes Yu Yu’s 虞预 *Jin shu* 晋书:

> “贺氏本姓庆氏。汉安帝时，避清河王讳，改曰贺氏。”

So the change was not made by He Qi himself; it had already happened earlier in his family line. The *Sanguozhi* commentary gives the reason as **avoiding the taboo on Liu Qing’s name**. The note does not fully explain why the particular character **He 贺** was chosen; later surname explanations often say **Qing 庆** and **He 贺** both had the sense “congratulate/celebrate,” so He was used as a substitute, but that specific rationale is not stated in the surviving Pei Songzhi note itself.

q: Ts'ao Ts'ao asked P'ei Ch'ien about Liu Pei's abilities. How did P'ei Ch'ien assess him?
reply:
**Conclusion:** Pei Qian judged Liu Bei to be a man who could stir up disorder in the Central Plains but was not suited to bring orderly governance there; however, if Liu Bei could seize an opportunity and hold strategic terrain, he could become the lord of one region.

**Evidence:** In the *Sanguozhi* (*Records of the Three Kingdoms*), in the *Wei Shu* biography of Pei Qian (《三国志·魏书·裴潜传》), Cao Cao asked Pei Qian:

> “卿前与刘备俱在荆州，卿以备才如何？”

Pei Qian replied:

> “使居中国，能乱人而不能为治也；若乘间守险，足为一方之主。”

Rough translation: “If he were placed in the Central States, he could create disorder among men, but he could not govern them well. If he seized an opportunity and held strategic passes/terrain, he would be sufficient to be the lord of one region.”

Cao Cao is then recorded as saying, “善” — “Good” / “Well said.”

So Pei Qian’s assessment was twofold: Liu Bei was dangerous and disruptive in the central heartland, but fully capable of becoming a regional power if he had terrain and opportunity.

q: When Du Xi was Chief of Xi'e county, a Jing Province army of more than ten thousand came to attack the town. How many people did he muster to defend it? How did the defense turn out? And in which year did this battle take place?
reply:
**Conclusion:** According to the *Sanguozhi* account, Du Xi did **not** have a stated total number of defenders mustered. He kept the able-bodied men for defense, and then selected **50 brave men** for a sortie. The defense succeeded: the Jing Province army of over 10,000 was thrown into confusion and withdrew. The exact year is **not given in Du Xi’s *Sanguozhi* biography**; the *Zizhi Tongjian* places it in **197 CE (Jian’an 2)**.

**Evidence from *Sanguozhi* (Du Xi’s biography):**  
Du Xi was made Chief of Xi’e. The county bordered the southern frontier and was troubled by bandits. He sent the old and weak back to farming and kept the strong men to prepare the defense. Then:

> “荆州遣兵万余人攻之，袭乃选壮士五十人，开城门击之，贼众惊乱，遂退。”

Translation: A Jing Province force of more than 10,000 attacked. Du Xi then selected 50 brave men, opened the city gate, and struck them. The enemy mass was startled and thrown into disorder, and withdrew.

After this, Cao Cao praised him and appointed him as **Yilang** (议郎).

So, strictly from *Sanguozhi*, the only number given is **50 brave men** used in the counterattack, not the total garrison. The year is not recorded there; if you use the *Zizhi Tongjian* chronology, it is **197 CE**.

q: Which painter, while painting a screen for Sun Quan, let a drop of ink fall on the silk by mistake and turned it into a fly — so lifelike that Sun Quan took it for a real fly and raised his hand to flick it away?
reply:
The painter was **Cao Buxing** (曹不兴; pinyin: **Cao Buxing**), also written **Cao Fuxing** (曹弗兴), a painter of Eastern Wu.

Evidence: This anecdote is preserved in **Pei Songzhi’s commentary** to the *Sanguozhi*, quoting the *Wu Lu* (《吴录》): Cao Buxing was from Wuxing. **Sun Quan** had him paint a screen; by mistake he let a dot of ink fall on the white silk, then turned it into a fly. Sun Quan took it for a real fly and raised his hand to flick it away.

Note: This story is **not in Chen Shou’s main text** of the *Sanguozhi*; it belongs to Pei Songzhi’s commentary and the later painting-legend tradition.

q: A woman from Jiuquan avenged her father by stabbing his killer to death in broad daylight in front of the city post-house, then went to the county office and gave herself up. Who was she, and in which year did this happen?
reply:
She was **Zhao E** (赵娥), also referred to as **Pang E-qin** (庞娥亲), the mother of **Pang Yu** (庞淯). The killing took place in **179 CE**, the **2nd year of the Guanghe era** (光和二年) of Emperor Ling of Han.

Evidence: In the *Sanguozhi*, in the biography of Pang Yu (Wei shu 18), Pei Songzhi’s commentary quotes Huangfu Mi’s *Lienü zhuan*. It says her father, **Zhao Jun’an** (赵君安) of Lufu, was killed by **Li Shou** (李寿) of the same county. Her brothers died in an epidemic, so she prepared weapons and waited for years. In **Guanghe 2 (179 CE)** she encountered Li Shou at the **duting** (都亭, the city post-house/ward pavilion), stabbed him to death in daylight, and then went to the county office to surrender. The *Hou Han Shu* “Lienü zhuan” also preserves the same story.

q: A wealthy man gave a ride to a woman on the road. She told him she was a messenger from Heaven sent to burn down his house, but because he had been kind to her she let him go home first and move his valuables out. Who was this wealthy man?
reply:
The wealthy man was **Mi Zhu** (糜竺, **Mí Zhú**), courtesy name **Zizhong** (子仲).

**Basis:** In the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* story, Mi Zhu was a very rich man from Donghai. On the road he kindly gave a woman a ride. She revealed that she was a heavenly messenger—in the *Romance* version, the **South Fire Virtue Star Lord** (南方火德星君)—sent to burn down his house. Because he had treated her courteously, she warned him to go home first and move his valuables out. His house later burned.

**Historical note:** Chen Shou’s main text in the *San Guo Zhi* biography of Mi Zhu says he came from a wealthy merchant family and was enormously rich, but it does **not** contain this woman/fire story. The anecdote is found in **Pei Songzhi’s commentary**, which quotes the *Sou Shen Ji* (搜神记). There the woman says she is a “heavenly messenger” sent to burn Mi Zhu’s house, and she warns him because he gave her a ride. So the core identification is **Mi Zhu**; the supernatural detail belongs to the anecdotal/Romance tradition rather than Chen Shou’s main historical text.

q: A soldier who went out and never came back was treated as a deserter, and his wife and children were made government slaves. His wife protested everywhere without success. Which Commandant of Justice eventually discovered that the soldier had been murdered for money by a man from his own camp, and who was the murderer?
reply:
The Commandant of Justice was **Gao Rou** (**Gao Rou**, 廷尉), and the murderer was **Jiao Ziwen** (**Jiao Ziwen**), a fellow soldier in the same camp as the missing soldier **Dou Li** (**Dou Li**).

According to the *Sanguozhi*, Wei Shu, biography of Gao Rou: Dou Li went out and did not return. His camp treated him as a deserter, and his wife **Ying** and their children were made government slaves. Ying appealed everywhere but no one would hear her, so she finally went to the Commandant of Justice. Gao Rou questioned her and learned that Dou Li had lent money to a fellow soldier named Jiao Ziwen and had been unable to get it back. Jiao Ziwen happened to be in prison on a minor charge. Gao Rou interrogated him, caught his changed expression, and pressed him until Jiao Ziwen confessed that he had killed Dou Li for money and told where the body was buried. The body was recovered, and Ying and her children were restored to commoner status.

So: **Commandant of Justice = Gao Rou; murderer = Jiao Ziwen.**

q: In the first year of Huangwu, the Wu fleet ran into a great storm at Dongkou and many ships capsized. Men in the water clung to the big ships and cried for help, but the other ships pushed them off with halberds and spears. Who ordered that those in the water be hauled aboard, and how many were saved?
reply:
**Conclusion:** The man who ordered the rescue was **Wu Can (吾粲, Wú Càn)**. According to the *Sanguozhi*, he saved **several hundred people**—not an exact number.

**Evidence:** In the *Sanguozhi*, *Wu Shu*, biography of **Wu Can**, it says that in the first year of **Huangwu** (222 CE), Wu Can, together with **Lü Fan** and **He Qi**, led the Wu fleet against Wei forces under **Cao Xiu** at **Dongkou**. A great wind broke the ships’ cables; many ships were capsized or driven ashore and lost. Wu Can’s ship alone remained intact. He then sent boats to rescue the drowning men, and “those saved numbered several hundred” (**所活数百人**).

So: **Wu Can ordered the rescue; the number saved was “several hundred,” not a precise figure.** The detail about other ships pushing drowning men away with halberds and spears belongs to the same anecdotal tradition; the main *Sanguozhi* text records Wu Can’s rescue and the phrase “所活数百人.”

q: An official of Shu-Han dreamed that a mulberry tree grew out of a well. The dream interpreter told him he would not live past forty-eight, and sure enough he died at forty-eight. Who was this official, and who interpreted the dream?
reply:
The official was **He Zhi** (何祗, Hé Zhī), courtesy name **Junsu** (君肃). The dream interpreter was **Zhao Zhi** (赵直, Zhào Zhí).

According to **Pei Songzhi’s annotation** to Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi*, in the biography of **Yang Hong** (杨洪), quoting the *Yibu Qijiu Zhuan* (《益部耆旧传》), He Zhi once dreamed that a mulberry tree grew out of a well. He asked Zhao Zhi about it. Zhao Zhi said:

> “A mulberry is not something that belongs in a well; it will surely be transplanted. But the character *sang* 桑 can be read as ‘forty-eight’; I fear your lifespan will not exceed this.”

He Zhi laughed and said, “That is enough.” He died at the age of forty-eight, exactly as predicted.

q: A man opened up wasteland at Yongxing and planted twenty-odd mu of rice. Just as it was ripening, a local claimed it as his own; the man simply let him have the rice, and when the county Chief wanted to punish the local, he even pleaded on his behalf. Who was this man?
reply:
The man was **Zhongli Mu** (courtesy name **Zigan**), a man from **Shanyin** in **Kuaiji** and later an official/general of Eastern Wu.

According to the **Records of the Three Kingdoms**, in the **Wu Book**, “Biography of Zhongli Mu”:

When Zhongli Mu was young, he lived at **Yongxing**, personally reclaimed wasteland, and planted over twenty *mu* of rice. When the rice was about to ripen, a local resident claimed it as his own. Zhongli Mu simply said, in effect, “I reclaimed it only because the land was waste,” and gave him the rice. The county chief heard about this, arrested the local man, and wanted to punish him according to law. Zhongli Mu pleaded on the man’s behalf. The county chief refused at first, so Zhongli Mu prepared to leave and return to Shanyin. The chief then went to stop him and released the local man.

Later the local man, ashamed and fearful, hulled the rice he had taken and got **sixty *hu*** of rice, which he tried to return to Zhongli Mu. Zhongli Mu shut his door and would not accept it. The man left it by the roadside, and no one took it. Because of this, Zhongli Mu became well known.

So the answer is **Zhongli Mu**.

q: During the Incident at the Gaoping Tombs, when Sima Yi removed Cao Shuang, which two ministers did he send to take over the camps of Cao Shuang and Cao Xi respectively, and what did Sima Yi say to one of them?
reply:
During the Gaopingling coup in 249, Sima Yi sent:

- **Gao Rou** (高柔), then **Situ** (司徒, Minister over the Masses), to take over **Cao Shuang’s** camp.
- **Wang Guan** (王观), then **Taipu** (太仆, Minister Coachman), to take over **Cao Xi’s** camp.

To one of them — **Gao Rou** — Sima Yi said:

> **“Jun wei Zhou Bo yi.”**  
> **君为周勃矣。**  
> “You are now Zhou Bo.”

The point of the remark was to compare Gao Rou to the Han statesman **Zhou Bo** (周勃), who had taken control of the army in a dangerous political crisis.

Evidence: This detail is not in Chen Shou’s main text of the *Sanguozhi*; it appears in **Pei Songzhi’s commentary** to the *Cao Shuang zhuan*, quoting Gan Bao’s *Jin Ji*:  
“宣王使高柔假节行大将军事，据爽营；王观行中领军事，据羲营。宣王谓柔曰：‘君为周勃矣。’”

q: Which Cavalier Regular Palace Attendant of Wu got drunk and collapsed at the banquet Sun Hao held for Ding Zhong on his return from an embassy to Jin, and was beheaded in the hall on Sun Hao's orders? In which year?
reply:
The man was **Wang Fan** (王蕃; **Wang Fan**), whose courtesy name was **Yongyuan** (永元). He was a **散骑常侍** (Cavalier Regular Palace Attendant) of Wu. The year was **266 CE**, i.e. Wu’s **Ganlu 2** (甘露二年; also Jin’s Taishi 2).

Evidence: In the *Sanguozhi*, *Wu Shu*, *Sun Hao zhuan*, it is recorded that Sun Hao sent **Ding Zhong** (丁忠) on an embassy to Jin; when Ding Zhong returned, Sun Hao held a great banquet for the officials. Wang Fan became drunk and collapsed. Sun Hao suspected he was feigning, and ordered him beheaded in the hall. Wang Fan’s own biography in *Wu Shu* 20 gives further detail: he was drunk and prostrate, was carried out, then called back, and because he was still drunk Sun Hao angrily had him executed in the hall; he was then 39 years old.

q: How many different people named Zhao Da appear in the Records of the Three Kingdoms, and what did each of them do?
reply:
**Conclusion:** In the *Sanguozhi* main text plus Pei Songzhi’s commentary, I can identify only **one distinct person named Zhao Da (赵达, Zhao Da)**. He was a **Wu diviner/astrologer/calculation specialist** under **Sun Quan (孙权, Sun Quan)**, not a general or major official. I cannot verify a second, different Zhao Da in the *Sanguozhi* / Pei Songzhi corpus.

**What he did, according to the record:**

q: Who were the 'Eight Masters of Wu', and what was each of them famous for?
reply:
Short answer: the “Eight Masters of Wu” usually means the **“Eight Excellences of Wu”** (*Wu ba jue*), not a formal office or school. The list comes from Pei Songzhi’s commentary to the *Sanguozhi*, quoting Zhang Bo’s *Wu Lu*. The eight were:

| Person | Famous for |
|---|---|
| **Huang Xiang** | Calligraphy |
| **Yan Wu** | Go/weiqi; said to have no equal in his generation |
| **Song Shou** | Dream interpretation / oneiromancy |
| **Cao Buxing** | Painting |
| **Zheng Yu** | Physiognomy / face-reading |
| **Wu Fan** | Calendrical arts and wind/weather omens; the *Wu Lu* list labels him as skilled in “wind observation” |
| **Liu Dun** | Astronomy, omens, and divination; the list labels him as skilled in “qi observation” |
| **Zhao Da** | Arithmetic and mathematical divination, especially the “Nine Palaces One Calculation” method |

Evidence: the *Sanguozhi* volume 63 has separate biographies of **Wu Fan**, **Liu Dun**, and **Zhao Da**. Wu Fan is described as “skilled in calendrical calculation and knowing wind/qi”; Liu Dun as “understanding heavenly offices and reaching the arts of divination,” especially *Taiyi*; Zhao Da as practicing “the art of Nine Palaces One Calculation,” able to calculate hidden numbers and answer as if divine. Pei Songzhi’s note quoting the *Wu Lu* then says that Wu Fan, Liu Dun, Zhao Da, Yan Wu, Song Shou, Cao Buxing, Huang Xiang, and Zheng Yu “were known in their generation as the Eight Excellences.” The other five are known mainly from this annotation and related notes, not from separate main biographies in Chen Shou’s text.

If by “Eight Masters of Wu” you meant some other label such as “Eight Worthies/Talents” (*ba jun*) of Wu, that would be a different list; the common identification is the *Wu ba jue* above.

q: Who had the courtesy name Wenze?
reply:
Yu Jin (于禁, pinyin: Yu Jin) had the courtesy name Wenze (文则).

Source: In the *Sanguozhi* (《三国志》), *Wei Shu* biography of Yu Jin, it says: “于禁字文则，泰山钜平人也” — “Yu Jin, courtesy name Wenze, was a man from Juping in Taishan.”

q: Who was the man that Kuan Yü's troops called the 'White Horse General' (Baima jiangjun)?
reply:
The man was **Pang De** (**Páng Dé**, 庞德), courtesy name **Lingming** (令明).

**Conclusion:** In the *Sanguozhi* account, Guan Yu’s troops called **Pang De** the “White Horse General” (**Báimǎ Jiāngjūn**, 白马将军) because he often rode a white horse into battle.

**Evidence:** 《三国志·魏书十八·庞德传》 says:

> “时德常乘白马，羽军谓之白马将军，皆惮之。”

Translation: “At that time Pang De often rode a white horse; Guan Yu’s troops called him the White Horse General, and all feared him.”

Pang De was serving Cao Cao under Cao Ren at Fancheng. He fought Guan Yu, shot Guan Yu in the forehead, and was later captured when the Han River flooded; he refused to surrender and was killed by Guan Yu.

So in this specific context, the “White Horse General” was **Pang De**, not Gongsun Zan, who is also associated with white horses in other contexts.

q: In the course of pacifying the Shanyue, which new counties did He Qi successively petition to have established?
reply:
**Conclusion:** In the *Sanguozhi* account of He Qi’s campaigns against the Shanyue, the new counties he successively petitioned to establish were:

1. **Shixin xian 始新县** — from **Yexiang 叶乡**.
2. **Xinding xian 新定县**
3. **Liyang xian 黎阳县** — some editions/sources write **犁阳**.
4. **Xiuyang xian 休阳县**

These were created by splitting **She xian 歙县**; together with the existing **Yi 黟**, **She 歙**, and the new **Shixin 始新**, they formed **Xindu jun 新都郡**.

If one counts the earlier Shanyue-related campaign too, He Qi also “divided Shangrao to make **Jianping xian 建平县**,” but the text does not explicitly say he “petitioned” (*biao* 表) for that one.

**Evidence from *Sanguozhi·Wu Shu·He Qi Zhuan*:**
- “齐表言以叶乡为始新县” — He Qi petitioned to make Yexiang into Shixin County.
- “齐复表分歙为新定、黎阳、休阳，并黟、歙、始新，凡六县，权遂割为新都郡” — He Qi again petitioned to split She into Xinding, Liyang, and Xiuyang; with Yi, She, and Shixin, these six counties became Xindu Commandery.
- Earlier: “十年，转讨上饶，分以为建平县” — in Jian’an 10 he campaigned against Shangrao and divided it to establish Jianping County, though this is not phrased as a “petition” in the same way.

q: Who was the Marquis of Panyu, and for what achievement was he given that title?
reply:
**Conclusion:** The Marquis of Panyu (番禺侯, Panyu Hou) was **Lü Dai** (吕岱, Lǚ Dài), a general of Eastern Wu. He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Panyu mainly for his achievement in **pacifying Jiaozhou and extending Wu influence into the south**.

**Evidence from the *Sanguozhi*:** In the *Wu Shu*, biography of Lü Dai, after Shi Xie (士燮) died and Shi Hui (士徽) resisted Wu control in Jiaozhou, Sun Quan sent Lü Dai as inspector of Jiaozhou. Lü Dai defeated and executed Shi Hui, pacifying Jiaozhi. He then attacked Jiuzhen (九真), and sent officials south to proclaim Wu’s authority to places such as Funan (扶南), Linyi (林邑), and Tangming (堂明); their rulers sent envoys with tribute. The text says Sun Quan praised his merit, promoted him to General Who Guards the South (镇南将军), and enfeoffed him as **Marquis of Panyu**.

This title is historical, not merely a *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* invention. The novel may treat Lü Dai as a minor Wu general, but the *Sanguozhi* record is as above. I am not certain of the exact year from memory; the context is after Shi Xie’s death and the Jiaozhou campaigns.

q: Why was Wei Zhao put to death by Sun Hao?
reply:
**Conclusion:** According to the *Sanguozhi* account, Sun Hao (孙皓) had Wei Zhao (韦昭/韦曜) executed because Wei Zhao repeatedly refused to gratify Sun Hao’s wishes. The decisive issue was Wei Zhao’s refusal to write Sun Hao’s father, Sun He (孙和), into the official history as a *benji* 本纪 (“imperial annals”). Wei Zhao insisted that Sun He had never actually ascended the throne, so he should be given only a *liezhuan* 列传 (“ordinary biography”). Sun Hao was enraged. Combined with Wei Zhao’s resistance to Sun Hao’s forced-drinking banquets and his criticism of court humiliations, Sun Hao treated him as disobedient and disloyal, imprisoned him, and—despite Hua He’s 华覈 plea—executed him.

**Evidence from *Sanguozhi*:**

1. **The history-writing dispute:**  
   The *Sanguozhi·Wu shu·Wei Yao zhuan* says:  
   > “皓欲为父和作纪，曜固执以为和未登帝位，宜为传。皓怒。”  
   Sun Hao wanted to make a *benji* for his father Sun He; Wei Zhao stubbornly argued that Sun He had not ascended the throne and should be a *liezhuan*. Sun Hao was angry.

2. **The banquet issue:**  
   Sun Hao held all-day drinking parties and required officials to drink seven *sheng* 升, even forcing those who could not drink to pour it out. Wei Zhao normally could not drink more than two *sheng*. At first, when still in favor, Sun Hao secretly gave him tea as a substitute. Later, when Wei Zhao fell out of favor, Sun Hao forced him and used his refusal as a crime. Sun Hao also had attendants mock and expose officials’ private faults at banquets; Wei Zhao considered this damaging and improper.

3. **Sun Hao’s stated reason:**  
   The biography says Sun Hao  
   > “以为不承用诏命，意不忠尽，遂积前后事，收曜付狱。”  
   He thought Wei Zhao did not accept and carry out his orders and was not fully loyal; therefore he accumulated these offenses and had Wei Zhao arrested.

4. **Execution:**  
   Hua He submitted a memorial begging for mercy, but Sun Hao refused. The text says:  
   > “皓不许，遂诛曜，徙其家属于零陵。曜时年七十。”  
   Sun Hao would not permit it, executed Wei Zhao, and exiled his family to Lingling. Wei Zhao was then seventy years old.

**Note on the name:** In the received *Sanguozhi*, he often appears as **Wei Yao 韦曜** because Chen Shou avoided the Jin taboo on Sima Zhao’s 司马昭 name; the person is **Wei Zhao 韦昭**. This is the historical *Sanguozhi* account; I am not aware of a major *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* variant that changes the basic reason for his death.

q: When Mi Chu married his sister to Liu Pei, how many retainers and how much property did he contribute along with her?
reply:
**Short answer:** This is the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* version. In the novel, Mi Zhu (Mi Chu) gave his sister to Liu Bei as wife and contributed **3,000 servants/retainers**, plus **500 taels/ounces of gold and silver, 100,000 cash, 1,000 bolts of silk, and 1,000 measures of grain**.

**In the official history (*Sanguozhi*):**  
The *Sanguozhi*, “Mi Zhu zhuan,” says only:

> “竺于是进妹于先主为夫人，奴客二千，金银货币以助军资；于时困匮，赖此复振。”  
> “Mi Zhu then presented his sister to the Former Lord [Liu Bei] as his wife, with **2,000 slaves/retainers**, and gold, silver, and coin to support military expenses. At that time Liu Bei was in desperate straits and relied on this to revive.”

So the **Sanguozhi** gives **2,000 “奴客”** but **does not record the exact amount** of gold, silver, or money. The earlier statement that Mi Zhu’s family had “僮客万人，赀产钜亿” — 10,000 servants/retainers and enormous wealth — describes the family’s general wealth, not the specific marriage contribution.

Thus: **Romance = 3,000 retainers and a detailed list of property; official history = 2,000 retainers and unspecified gold/silver/coin.**

q: How did Xu Zhu realize that Xu Ta and the others were plotting to assassinate Cao Cao? And how did he deal with them?
reply:
**Conclusion:** In the *Sanguozhi* account, Xu Chu did **not** discover the plot through prior intelligence or investigation. He felt a sudden unease/premonition after going to his rest quarters, returned to Cao Cao’s side, and then saw that Xu Ta and the others were shocked to find him there. He immediately killed them.

**Evidence:** This story is in *Sanguozhi*, Wei shu, juan 18, *Xu Chu zhuan*. The main text says, in paraphrase:

> Xu Chu followed Cao Cao in the campaign against Yuan Shao. At that time Xu Ta and others plotted treason. Because Xu Chu constantly attended Cao Cao, they feared to act. They waited for a day when Xu Chu went down to rest. When Xu Chu reached the rest quarters, his heart moved/ he felt a sudden unease, so he immediately returned to attend Cao Cao. Xu Ta and the others did not know this; they entered the tent with knives hidden on them. When they saw Xu Chu, they were greatly startled. Xu Chu noticed this and immediately killed Xu Ta and the others. Cao Cao trusted him even more.

So:

- **How he realized it:** not by deduction, but by a sudden feeling of unease (“心动”) and then by their panicked reaction when they saw him.
- **How he dealt with them:** he struck them down on the spot, killing Xu Ta and his confederates.
- **Aftermath:** Cao Cao became even more trusting of Xu Chu.

Note: I take “Xu Zhu” to mean **Xu Chu** (许褚), and “Xu Ta” to be **Xu Ta** (徐他). This episode is from the standard history. I am not certain of a separate *Romance* version of this specific Xu Ta episode.

q: What happened when Zhuge Liang used the Empty Fort Strategy at Yangping to scare off Sima Yi?
reply:
**Conclusion:** In Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi* main text, there is **no record** that Zhuge Liang used an “empty fort” at Yangping to scare off Sima Yi. The Yangping empty-fort story appears only in **Pei Songzhi’s annotation**, quoting an anecdote attributed to **Guo Chong**; Pei Songzhi himself rejects it as unreliable. The famous empty-fort scene in *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* is set at **Xicheng**, not Yangping, and is a literary invention.

**The Yangping anecdote as quoted by Pei Songzhi:**  
Guo Chong’s story says that Zhuge Liang was at Yangping with only about 10,000 men, having sent Wei Yan and other troops east. Sima Yi allegedly came with a reported 200,000 troops. When scouts told Sima Yi that Zhuge Liang’s force was weak, Zhuge Liang ordered his men to lower flags, silence drums, open the city gates, and calmly sweep and sprinkle water. Sima Yi, believing Zhuge Liang was always cautious, suspected an ambush and withdrew toward the hills. The next day Zhuge Liang laughed and said Sima Yi must have thought there was a strong ambush. Sima Yi later regretted it.

**Why this is not accepted as history:**  
Pei Songzhi, after quoting this, points out that the chronology does not fit. At the time in question, Sima Yi was not facing Zhuge Liang at Yangping, and the story conflicts with other known records, including Wei Yan’s role. Pei therefore judges the anecdote unreliable. So in the *Sanguozhi* proper, Zhuge Liang did **not** scare off Sima Yi with an empty fort at Yangping.

**Romance vs. history:**  
In *Romance*, after the defeat at Jieting, Zhuge Liang is at Xicheng with a tiny force; he opens the gates and plays the qin on the city tower. Sima Yi suspects an ambush and retreats. That is the novel’s famous “empty fort” scene. Historically, no such event is recorded in Chen Shou’s main text. Sima Yi did face Zhuge Liang later, especially in 231 and 234, but not in this empty-fort episode.

q: In the Battle of Bowang, how did Zhuge Liang set the fire ambush against Xiahou Dun?
reply:
**Conclusion:** In the official histories, Zhuge Liang did **not** set any fire ambush against Xiahou Dun at Bowang. That is the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* version. Historically, the Battle of Bowang was fought by **Liu Bei** before Zhuge Liang joined him. Liu Bei used fire as part of a feigned retreat and then ambushed Xiahou Dun.

**Official-history evidence:**

- In Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi*, *Liu Bei zhuan* (先主传), the record says roughly: Liu Bei set hidden troops; he himself burned his camp and pretended to flee; Xiahou Dun and others pursued, and were defeated by the ambush.
- In *Li Dian zhuan* (李典传), the account is fuller: Liu Bei burned his camp and withdrew. Li Dian warned, “The enemy retreats without reason; there must be an ambush. The southern road is narrow, with deep grass and trees—do not pursue.” Xiahou Dun did not listen and pursued with Yu Jin, while Li Dian stayed behind. Xiahou Dun and Yu Jin indeed entered the ambush and were defeated; Li Dian came to their rescue, and Liu Bei withdrew when he saw the relief force arrive.
- Pei Songzhi’s annotations do not add any role for Zhuge Liang in this battle.

So in the official record: the fire was **Liu Bei burning his own camp to fake a retreat**, and the ambush was **Liu Bei’s**, not Zhuge Liang’s.

**Romance version:** In *Sanguo Yanyi*, the famous “fire at Bowangpo” is made Zhuge Liang’s first military exploit. He arranges Zhao Yun to lure Xiahou Dun, then uses Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, and fire to ambush him. That is literary invention. Historically, Zhuge Liang was not present at Bowang; he joined Liu Bei later. The exact year of the battle is uncertain, but it was before Zhuge Liang’s recruitment.

q: A strategic proposal called for first occupying Jing and Yi Provinces, allying with Sun Quan, waiting for a change in the situation in the north, and then advancing along two routes. If Jing Province were lost, which key precondition of this strategy would no longer hold?
reply:
**Conclusion:** If **Jing Province** were lost, the key precondition that no longer held was **Liu Bei’s possession of both Jing and Yi Provinces as the two-base foundation for a two-route advance**. In particular, the planned **eastern route from Jing toward Wan and Luo** could no longer be launched. If Jing was lost to **Sun Quan**, then the related precondition of **“allying with Sun Quan”** also collapsed.

**Evidence:** In the *Sanguozhi*, *Zhuge Liang zhuan*, the Longzhong plan says:

> “若跨有荆、益……天下有变，则命一上将将荆州之军以向宛、洛，将军身率益州之众出于秦川。”

That is: hold **Jing** and **Yi**, ally with **Sun Quan**, wait for change in the north, then send one army from **Jing** toward **Wan/Luo** and another from **Yi** toward **Qinchuan**. So the two-pronged strategy presupposes holding **Jing** as one of the two bases. Without Jing, only the Yi route remains, and the pincer plan is broken.

Historically, after **Sun Quan**’s forces under **Lü Meng** seized Jing and **Guan Yu** was killed, the Sun–Liu alliance effectively broke down, and **Liu Bei**’s later campaign against Wu ended in defeat. Thus both the geographic precondition and, in practice, the alliance precondition were lost.

q: What is the story of Kuan Yü killing Ts'ai Yang at Ku-ch'eng?
reply:
**Conclusion:** The story of Guan Yu killing Cai Yang at Gucheng is from *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* (《三国演义》), not from the official *Sanguozhi*. In the novel, Guan Yu kills Cai Yang to prove his loyalty to Zhang Fei. In the official history, Cai Yang was sent by Cao Cao against Liu Bei in Runan and was killed by **Liu Bei**, not by Guan Yu at Gucheng.

**Romance version:**  
In Chapter 28, “Zhan Cai Yang xiongdi shiyi, hui Gucheng zhongchen juyi” (“斩蔡阳兄弟释疑 会古城主臣聚义”), Guan Yu is escorting Liu Bei’s wives and reaches Gucheng (Ku-ch’eng). Zhang Fei is holding the city and suspects Guan Yu has truly submitted to Cao Cao. Just then Cai Yang arrives in pursuit—in the novel, he is connected to Qin Qi, whom Guan Yu had killed at the Yellow River, and wants revenge. Zhang Fei challenges Guan Yu to prove himself by killing Cai Yang. Guan Yu does so, and Zhang Fei finally accepts him. Later Liu Bei and others reunite with them at Gucheng.

**Official history:**  
The *Sanguozhi*, Shu Shu, “Xianzhu Zhuan” (《三国志·蜀书·先主传》) says that Yuan Shao sent Liu Bei back to Runan, where Liu Bei joined Gong Du and others. Cao Cao then sent Cai Yang to attack him:

> “曹公遣蔡阳击之，为先主所杀。”  
> “Cao Cao sent Cai Yang to attack him; he was killed by the Former Lord [Liu Bei].”

So in the received *Sanguozhi* text, **Cai Yang was killed by Liu Bei at Runan**, not by Guan Yu at Gucheng. Guan Yu’s own biography records that he left Cao Cao, sealed up Cao Cao’s gifts, wrote a farewell, and returned to Liu Bei; Cao Cao said, “Each serves his own lord; do not pursue him.” It does **not** contain a Gucheng duel with Cai Yang. I am not aware of a Pei Songzhi note that supplies this Gucheng/Cai Yang story either.

So: **Romance = Guan Yu kills Cai Yang at Gucheng; history = Liu Bei kills Cai Yang at Runan.**

q: This man originally served under Liu Zhang but later became one of Liu Bei's key advisers. He helped plan the seizure of Yi Province and accompanied Liu Bei in the contest for Hanzhong. He died of illness before Liu Bei did, and so had no part in the deathbed entrustment. Who was he?
reply:
The man was **Fa Zheng** (法正), courtesy name **Xiaozhi** (孝直).

**Evidence from the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*:**

- In the *Shu Shu* biography of **Fa Zheng**, he first entered Yi Province under **Liu Zhang** (刘璋), serving as a military adviser but feeling underused. He and **Zhang Song** (张松) secretly planned to bring in **Liu Bei**.
- When Liu Zhang sent Fa Zheng to meet Liu Bei, Fa Zheng privately advised Liu Bei to seize Yi Province, saying that with Liu Zhang’s weakness and internal support, the enterprise could succeed “as easily as turning one’s palm.”
- During the **Hanzhong campaign**, the *Fa Zheng zhuan* says Liu Bei followed his strategy and that **Fa Zheng also accompanied the army** (“正亦从行”). At **Dingjun Mountain**, Fa Zheng advised the attack that led to **Xiahou Yuan**’s death.
- After Liu Bei became **King of Hanzhong** in 219, he appointed Fa Zheng as **Shangshu Ling** (尚书令). Fa Zheng died the next year, in 220, at age 45. Liu Bei wept for him for days.
- Liu Bei died in 223 at **Baidicheng**, where his deathbed entrustment went to **Zhuge Liang** and **Li Yan**. Fa Zheng had already died, so he had no part in it.
- After Liu Bei’s defeat at **Yiling**, Zhuge Liang sighed: “If **Fa Xiaozhi** were alive, he could have restrained the sovereign from going east; even if he went east, he would not have been in such danger.” This confirms Fa Zheng died before that crisis.

So the answer is **Fa Zheng (法正, Fa Zheng)**.

q: This man first served Yüan Shao and later went over to Ts'ao Ts'ao. He fought in Han-chung, defeated Ma Su at Chieh-t'ing, and finally died at Mu-men while pursuing the Shu army. Who was he?
reply:
The man is **Zhang He** (张郃), pinyin **Zhang He**, courtesy name **Junyi** (儁乂), a general of **Cao Wei**.

**Evidence from the *Sanguozhi*:**
- Zhang He’s biography in *Wei Shu* says he was first under **Han Fu**; after Han Fu was defeated, he went over to **Yuan Shao**, and later, during the Guandu campaign, he defected to **Cao Cao**. So if the question says he “first served Yuan Shao,” that is a slight simplification: strictly, he first served Han Fu, then Yuan Shao.
- In **228**, during Zhuge Liang’s northern expedition, Zhang He was sent against **Ma Su** at **Jieting** and heavily defeated him.
- He had earlier fought in **Hanzhong**, where he served alongside Xiahou Yuan and others after Cao Cao took Hanzhong from Zhang Lu.
- In **231**, while pursuing Zhuge Liang’s retreating Shu army, Zhang He reached **Mumen**. According to the *Sanguozhi*, he fought Zhuge Liang’s troops there, was hit by a flying arrow in the right knee, and died.

**Novel vs. history:** The identity is the same in the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*. The novel dramatizes his death at Mumen as an ambush; the *Sanguozhi* simply says he was struck by an arrow in the right knee and died there.

q: One side had the advantage in troops and supplies; the other, in a prolonged standoff, was running short of grain. In the end the weaker side, acting on intelligence from a defector, raided the enemy's main grain depot and turned the battle around. Which battle was this, and who was the defector?
reply:
**Conclusion:** This was the **Battle of Guandu** (Guandu zhi zhan, 官渡之战), around 200 CE, between **Cao Cao** and **Yuan Shao**. The defector was **Xu You** (许攸), a Yuan Shao adviser who came over to Cao Cao. His intelligence led Cao Cao to raid Yuan Shao’s main grain depot, traditionally called **Wuchao** (乌巢), guarded by **Chunyu Qiong** (淳于琼). Cao Cao’s night raid burned the grain and turned the campaign around.

**Evidence from the _Sanguozhi_:**

- Chen Shou’s main text in the _Wei shu · Wudi ji_ says:  
  > “绍谋臣许攸贪财，绍不能足，来奔，因说公击琼等。”  
  Translation: “Yuan Shao’s adviser Xu You was greedy for wealth, and Yuan Shao could not satisfy him; he came to defect, and therefore advised Cao Cao to attack Chunyu Qiong and the others.”

- The same passage then records Cao Cao’s raid:  
  > “公乃留曹洪守，自将步骑五千人夜往……大破琼等，皆斩之。”  
  Translation: “Cao Cao then left Cao Hong to guard, personally led 5,000 infantry and cavalry by night… and heavily defeated Chunyu Qiong’s force, killing them all.”

- Pei Songzhi’s note quoting the _Cao Man zhuan_ adds details of the night attack and burning of the grain:  
  > “既至，围屯，大放火，营中惊乱。大破之，尽燔其粮谷宝货……”  
  Translation: “When they arrived, they surrounded the camp, set great fires, and the camp was thrown into panic. They heavily defeated them and burned all their grain and supplies.”

So the key defector is **Xu You (许攸)**. This core event is not a Romance-only invention; the _Sanguozhi_ records it. The Romance adds dramatic details, but the historical fact is that Xu You’s defection gave Cao Cao the intelligence to strike Yuan Shao’s grain depot.

q: Cao Cao took in Emperor Xian of Han and issued orders in the name of the Han central government. Compared with relying on military strength alone, what political advantage did this chiefly bring him?
reply:
**Conclusion:** The chief political advantage was **legitimacy** — the ability to turn raw military power into lawful central-government authority. By controlling Emperor Xian, Cao Cao could issue edicts, appoint and dismiss officials, grant titles, summon or condemn rivals, and present his wars as Han “royal campaigns” against rebels. Military strength alone could win battles, but it could not make him the lawful center of the empire.

**Evidence from the *Sanguozhi*:**

- **Mao Jie’s advice** in the *Mao Jie zhuan* states the program directly: Cao Cao should “**feng tianzi yi ling buchen**” — support the Son of Heaven in order to command those who are disloyal — and also build up agriculture and military supplies. Cao Cao accepted this advice. This is the clearest statement of the political advantage.

- **Xun Yu’s advice** in the *Xun Yu zhuan* says welcoming the emperor would let Cao Cao “**feng zhushang yi cong minwang**” (support the ruler to follow popular hopes), “**bing zhigong yi fu xiongjie**” (use impartiality to subdue the powerful), and “**fu hongyi yi zhi yingjun**” (uphold great righteousness to attract outstanding men). He warned that if Cao Cao delayed, “**si fang sheng xin**” — various quarters would form other plans. So the emperor gave Cao Cao popular legitimacy, authority over rivals, and a magnet for talent.

- In the *Wudi ji*, in 196 Cao Cao welcomed Emperor Xian, moved the court to Xu, and received from the emperor **jieyue** (节钺), **lushangshu shi** (录尚书事, control of memorials and edicts), and the titles **Grand General** and **Marquis of Wuping**. The text says: “Since the Son of Heaven had moved west, the court had daily grown chaotic; only now were the ancestral temples and state institutions established again.” This shows Cao Cao was not merely a warlord but the effective head of the Han central government.

- The same biography shows he used imperial appointments to manage rivals: he made **Yuan Shao** **Grand Commandant**, but Yuan Shao was ashamed to rank below Cao Cao, so Cao Cao yielded the title **Grand General** to Yuan Shao and took **Minister of Works** and **Acting General of Chariots and Cavalry**. This is a concrete example of using Han titles as political tools.

- In the *Yuan Shao zhuan*, after Cao Cao welcomed the emperor to Xu, he “**received the lands south of the Yellow River, and all the Guanzhong region attached itself to him**.” Yuan Shao regretted not taking the emperor first and asked Cao Cao to move the court closer to him; Cao Cao refused. This shows legitimacy translated into real political allegiance.

- In the *Zhuge Liang zhuan*, Zhuge Liang’s Longzhong dui describes Cao Cao as “**xie tianzi er ling zhuhou**” — “holding the Son of Heaven and commanding the feudal lords.” Contemporaries clearly saw this as the key reason Cao Cao could not be directly contested.

**Romance vs. history:** The Romance often uses the phrase “**xie tianzi yi ling zhuhou**” (挟天子以令诸侯). The *Sanguozhi* also contains this phrase in Zhuge Liang’s Longzhong dui. But Mao Jie’s advice in the *Sanguozhi* uses the more precise wording “**feng tianzi yi ling buchen**” — support the Son of Heaven to command the disloyal. The difference in wording reflects perspective, not a different fact: Cao Cao’s great political advantage was that he could define his allies as Han officials and his enemies as rebels.

q: Before the Battle of Red Cliffs, Liu Bei was comparatively weak, while Sun Quan held the Jiangdong territory and a navy. Given this imbalance, why did Sun Quan still have an incentive to ally with Liu Bei rather than stand by and let Cao Cao destroy him?
reply:
**Conclusion:** Sun Quan allied with Liu Bei not because Liu Bei was strong, but because letting Cao Cao destroy Liu Bei would have made Sun Quan’s own position worse. Liu Bei was a weak but useful buffer and co-belligerent: he still had some troops, Guan Yu’s water force, Liu Qi’s position at Jiangxia, and local connections in Jingzhou. More importantly, if Cao Cao absorbed Liu Bei and Jingzhou, he would gain Jingzhou’s fleet and the upper Yangtze, removing Sun Quan’s main geographic advantage and leaving Jiangdong to face Cao alone. For Sun Quan, alliance was a hard-headed defensive necessity.

**Evidence from the *Sanguozhi* and Pei Songzhi’s notes:**

1. **Cao Cao directly threatened Sun Quan.**  
   After Liu Cong surrendered Jingzhou, Cao Cao sent Sun Quan a letter. Pei Songzhi’s note in the *Sun Quan zhuan* quoting the *Jiang Biao zhuan* says Cao claimed he had trained a huge water army and would “hunt with you in Wu.” This made clear that neutrality or submission was not safe. Many of Sun Quan’s advisers urged surrender.

2. **Jingzhou’s navy was the key danger.**  
   In the *Zhou Yu zhuan*, the surrender faction argued that once Cao Cao took Jingzhou, he would control Liu Biao’s large fleet and come down the Yangtze by both water and land. Then the Yangtze would no longer be a reliable barrier for Sun Quan. So letting Cao destroy Liu Bei and take Jingzhou would directly weaken Sun Quan.

3. **Lu Su saw Liu Bei as a necessary partner.**  
   In the *Lu Su zhuan*, Lu Su advised Sun Quan that Liu Bei was a “枭雄” and Cao Cao’s enemy, and that if Liu Bei could cooperate with Liu Biao’s sons, Sun Quan should ally with him. Lu Su also made the personal point to Sun Quan: officials like himself could surrender to Cao and still get posts, but Sun Quan as a ruler would have nowhere safe to go. This was an existential argument.

4. **Zhou Yu argued Cao Cao could be beaten now.**  
   In the *Zhou Yu zhuan*, Zhou Yu listed Cao’s weaknesses: unrest in the north, rear threats such as Ma Chao and Han Sui, northern troops unused to naval warfare, winter supply problems, and disease. He asked for 30,000 troops to resist. Sun Quan agreed. Liu Bei’s forces would add to this and allow Sun Quan to fight forward rather than wait.

5. **Liu Bei still had real assets.**  
   In the *Zhuge Liang zhuan*, Zhuge Liang told Sun Quan that Liu Bei still had Guan Yu’s water force and returning soldiers, plus Liu Qi’s troops at Jiangxia. Exact totals are uncertain, but Liu Bei was not a negligible military factor. Liu Qi’s Jiangxia was also strategically placed between Cao Cao and Sun Quan.

6. **Standing by would have isolated Sun Quan.**  
   If Sun Quan had done nothing, Cao Cao would likely have destroyed Liu Bei, absorbed Liu Qi and Jingzhou, and then faced Sun Quan with Jingzhou’s fleet and the upper Yangtze. Sun Quan would have lost his buffer and much of his naval advantage. Allying with Liu Bei let him fight at Red Cliffs with a co-belligerent and keep Cao Cao out of the middle and lower Yangtze.

**Romance vs. history:** The *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* makes Zhuge Liang the master diplomat who talks Sun Quan into the alliance. Historically, Lu Su was the key initiator of contact with Liu Bei, and Zhou Yu was decisive in pushing Sun Quan to fight. Zhuge Liang did go to Wu as Liu Bei’s envoy, but the decision was ultimately Sun Quan’s and his advisers’ strategic choice, not a favor to Liu Bei.

q: This man did not personally lead the army that conquered Shu, yet he pushed the war of conquest forward while he controlled the Cao-Wei court. His son later replaced Cao-Wei and founded the Western Jin. Who was he?
reply:
The man was **Sima Zhao** (司马昭), posthumously **Emperor Wen of Jin**.

**Conclusion:** Sima Zhao controlled the Cao-Wei court and pushed forward the campaign that conquered Shu-Han in 263, but he did not personally command the army in the field. His son **Sima Yan** later forced Cao-Wei’s last emperor, **Cao Huan**, to abdicate and founded the **Western Jin** dynasty.

**Evidence from the histories:**
- In *Sanguozhi*, the Wei annals for the last Wei emperor, **Cao Huan**, record that in **Jingyuan 4 (263)** the Wei court launched the campaign against Shu. The actual field commanders were **Deng Ai**, **Zhong Hui**, and **Zhuge Xu**. Sima Zhao, as the real power at court, directed the decision and overall strategy from Luoyang.
- *Sanguozhi*, “Zhong Hui zhuan,” says that **“Wen Wang”** — i.e. Sima Zhao — wanted a great expedition against Shu, and that Zhong Hui supported the plan and helped assess terrain and circumstances. This shows Sima Zhao as the driving force behind the campaign.
- *Sanguozhi*, “Deng Ai zhuan,” records Deng Ai’s famous surprise march through Yinping and the surrender of **Liu Shan**. Zhong Hui’s biography records Zhong Hui’s main advance. Neither account has Sima Zhao personally leading the conquering army.
- After the conquest, Sima Zhao’s power was further formalized. *Sanguozhi*, the annals of Cao Huan, records Cao Huan’s abdication to the Jin heir in **Xianxi 2 / Taishi 1** — in Gregorian terms **265/266**. That heir was Sima Zhao’s son **Sima Yan**, who became the first emperor of Jin.

**Romance note:** In *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, Sima Zhao is likewise shown as the Wei regent ordering Zhong Hui and Deng Ai to attack Shu; the novel does not make him personally lead the Shu campaign. On this point, the novel and the histories broadly agree.

q: While Kuan Yü was attacking Fan in the north, Sun Ch'üan's side seized Chiang-ling and other places in his rear. Why could Kuan Yü still collapse so quickly overall, even though he had won a major victory on the northern front?
reply:
**Short answer:** Guan Yu collapsed quickly not because the northern victory was worthless, but because it was **incomplete** and because his whole army depended on Jingzhou. When Sun Quan took Jiangling/Gong’an and captured the soldiers’ families, Guan Yu lost his base, supplies, retreat line, and morale. At the same time Xu Huang was pressing him at Fan. So his army did not need to be destroyed in a great battle; it dissolved.

**What the records say:**

1. **The victory at Fan was not a conquest of Fan.**  
   In the *Sanguozhi* biography of Guan Yu, Guan Yu besieged Cao Ren at Fan. He won a spectacular victory when heavy rain flooded Yu Jin’s seven armies; Yu Jin surrendered and Pang De was killed. Guan Yu’s prestige became so great that Cao Cao reportedly considered moving the capital.  
   But Cao Ren still held Fan. Cao Cao then sent Xu Huang, and the record says Guan Yu **“could not take [Fan] and withdrew his army”** (羽不能克，引军退还). So by the time Sun Quan struck his rear, Guan Yu’s northern front was already stalled or being reversed.

2. **His rear had been deliberately weakened.**  
   The *Lu Xun zhuan* says Lu Xun wrote flattering letters to Guan Yu, making him feel safe about the east. Guan Yu then **“gradually withdrew troops to go to Fan”** (稍撤兵以赴樊). This left Jingzhou more vulnerable. Sun Quan had also been alienated: Guan Yu insulted Sun Quan’s marriage envoy and refused the marriage alliance. Wu accounts also say Guan Yu seized Sun Quan’s rice at Xiangguan, giving Sun a pretext.

3. **Key commanders in the rear surrendered almost at once.**  
   The *Guan Yu zhuan* says Mi Fang was at Jiangling and Shi Ren at Gong’an. Both had long resented Guan Yu’s contempt. When Guan Yu campaigned, they failed to supply him fully; Guan Yu threatened, “When I return, I will deal with them.” Fearing punishment, they accepted Sun Quan’s inducement and surrendered. So Jiangling and Gong’an fell without a hard defense.  
   In the *Romance*, Shi Ren is often called Fu Shiren; the historical *Sanguozhi* name is Shi Ren.

4. **Lü Meng’s surprise attack and psychological warfare destroyed morale.**  
   The *Lü Meng zhuan* says Lü Meng hid elite troops in boats, disguised soldiers as merchants, and seized Guan Yu’s river pickets so Guan Yu did not know of the attack. After taking Jiangling, Lü Meng treated Guan Yu’s soldiers’ families well, forbade looting, and gave medical care to the sick. When Guan Yu sent messengers back, the soldiers learned their families were safe and even better treated than before. The result, as the *Guan Yu zhuan* says, was: **“Guan Yu’s army then scattered”** (羽军遂散).

5. **He was caught in a pincer and got no timely relief.**  
   Cao Cao had been advised by Sima Yi and Jiang Ji to encourage Sun Quan to attack Guan Yu’s rear. So Cao Cao’s side pressed from the north with Xu Huang while Sun Quan attacked from the east/south. The *Liu Feng zhuan* says Guan Yu repeatedly called on Liu Feng and Meng Da in Shangyong for aid, but they refused, claiming the newly attached commanderies could not be disturbed. The sources do not record a timely relief force from Liu Bei reaching him. Whether Liu Bei planned one is uncertain from the extant records.

**So the basic reason is structural:** Guan Yu’s northern success made him more threatening to both Cao Cao and Sun Quan, but it did not give him a secure base. Once Sun Quan captured Jiangling and the families, Guan Yu’s soldiers had little reason to keep fighting, and he had no safe place to retreat to. The *Romance* emphasizes “carelessness lost Jingzhou” and Guan Yu’s arrogance; the *Sanguozhi* does record his arrogance and insults, but the rapid collapse is better explained by the loss of his base, families, supplies, and morale.

q: The Oath of the Peach Garden: after Liu Pei, Kuan Yü and Chang Fei swore brotherhood, what was the order of seniority among the three?
reply:
**Conclusion:** In the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* (*Sanguo Yanyi*), the seniority after the Peach Garden oath is: **Liu Bei eldest, Guan Yu second, Zhang Fei third**.  

**But historically**, the Peach Garden oath itself is not recorded in Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi*. The *Sanguozhi* does not give a formal sworn-brother seniority among the three. What it does say is:

- Liu Bei was the leader, and he was “as close as brothers” with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei:  
  *“先主与二人寝则同床，恩若兄弟。”*  
  (“The Former Lord slept on the same bed with the two men, and their affection was like that of brothers.”)

- Guan Yu was several years older than Zhang Fei, and Zhang Fei treated him as an elder brother:  
  *“羽年长数岁，飞兄事之。”*  
  (“Guan Yu was several years older; Zhang Fei served him as an elder brother.”)

So, from the *Sanguozhi*, we can confirm **Guan Yu was older than Zhang Fei**, and Liu Bei was their lord/leader. But the *Sanguozhi* does **not** clearly record whether Liu Bei was older than Guan Yu, nor does it describe an actual Peach Garden oath.

The familiar order — **Liu Bei first, Guan Yu second, Zhang Fei third** — is therefore the *Romance*’s literary arrangement, not a securely documented fact in the *Sanguozhi*.

q: A Cao-Wei emperor left Luoyang to pay respects at the imperial tombs, and a senior minister who had long pleaded illness seized the chance to take control of the capital and force the other regent to surrender his power. What event was this, and who set it in motion?
reply:
**Conclusion:** This was the **Gaopingling zhi bian** (Incident at Gaoping Tombs), in **249 CE**. It was set in motion by **Sima Yi**. The emperor was **Cao Fang**; the other regent forced to surrender power was **Cao Shuang**.

**What happened:** Cao Fang left Luoyang with Cao Shuang and his brothers to pay respects at **Gaopingling**, the tomb of Emperor Ming (**Cao Rui**). Sima Yi, who had long claimed illness and stayed out of court, suddenly acted in Luoyang: he controlled the city gates and arsenal, obtained the backing of Empress Dowager **Guo**, and sent a memorial accusing Cao Shuang. Cao Shuang surrendered his authority; shortly afterward he and his faction were executed.

**Evidence:** The *Sanguozhi*, Wei Shu, biography of Cao Shuang records that in the first month of the 10th year of Zhengshi [249], “the imperial carriage went to Gaopingling; Shuang and his brothers all accompanied. Sima Yi [there called Xuanwang] marshaled troops, first occupied the arsenal, then camped at the floating bridge over the Luo River and memorialized against Shuang.” Pei Songzhi’s commentary, quoting works such as *Wei Lue* and *Shiyu*, adds that Sima Yi had pretended illness, so Cao Shuang no longer guarded against him.

The *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* uses the same basic outline; its added oaths and dramatic details are literary embellishment, but the core event is historical.

q: Sequence of episodes: put the following in the order in which they occur in *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*: A. The Three Visits to the Thatched Cottage  B. The Battle of Guandu  C. The Oath of the Peach Garden  D. The Battle of Red Cliffs
reply:
**Conclusion:** In *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, the order is:

**C. The Oath of the Peach Garden → B. The Battle of Guandu → A. The Three Visits to the Thatched Cottage → D. The Battle of Red Cliffs**

**Basis in the novel:**  
- **C. Oath of the Peach Garden (Taoyuan Jieyi)** — Chapter 1, at the very beginning, when Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei swear brotherhood.  
- **B. Battle of Guandu (Guandu zhi Zhan)** — around Chapters 30, when Cao Cao defeats Yuan Shao.  
- **A. Three Visits to the Thatched Cottage (Sangu Maolu)** — Chapters 37–38, when Liu Bei visits Zhuge Liang three times.  
- **D. Battle of Red Cliffs (Chibi zhi Zhan)** — Chapters 43–50, after Liu Bei has Zhuge Liang and allies with Sun Quan against Cao Cao.

**Historical note:**  
- The **Peach Garden Oath** is a *Romance* invention. In Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi*, Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei are described as being as close as brothers, but there is no record of a formal oath in a peach garden.  
- Historically, Guandu was in **200**, the Three Visits are usually placed around **207–208** (the *Sanguozhi* says Liu Bei went three times before meeting Zhuge Liang, but the exact year is not fully certain), and Red Cliffs was in **208**.

q: Identify the person: when Cao Cao was routed at Wancheng, who held the camp gate and fought to the death to cover Cao Cao's retreat?
reply:
**Dian Wei (Dian Wei)**.

According to the *Sanguozhi* (Chen Shou), in the *Wei Shu* biography of Dian Wei: after Zhang Xiu rebelled at Wancheng, Cao Cao’s forces were defeated and withdrew. Dian Wei fought at the gate of the camp, preventing the rebels from entering. He and about ten remaining men fought to the death; Dian Wei killed many enemies, was wounded many times, and finally died “glaring and cursing” as he fought. Cao Cao escaped, and later wept when he learned of Dian Wei’s death.

In the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, the same person, **Dian Wei**, is credited with holding the gate and dying to cover Cao Cao’s retreat. The novel adds details such as Hu Che’er stealing Dian Wei’s twin halberds and getting him drunk; the *Sanguozhi* does not record that detail.

q: Shu-Han's main base was Yi Province, and its northern expeditions had to haul grain across the mountains to the front. Why did 'winning a battle at the front' not necessarily mean 'being able to hold the newly gained territory for long'?
reply:
**Short answer:** In the Qinling–Guanzhong theater, a battlefield win was only a tactical success. To *hold* newly gained territory, Shu-Han needed continuous food supply, garrison manpower, control of passes, and time to consolidate local control. Shu-Han’s Yi Province base was too far behind the mountains, and Wei had greater strategic depth. So a victory often ended in withdrawal once provisions ran out or Wei reinforced. This is exactly the pattern in Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi*.

**Evidence from the *Sanguozhi* and Pei Songzhi’s annotations:**

1. **Zhuge Liang’s campaigns repeatedly end with “food exhausted, withdraw.”**  
   In Chen Shou’s *Zhuge Liang zhuan*:
   - In 228 winter, Zhuge Liang besieged Chencang; Cao Zhen resisted. Chen Shou says: **“Liang’s food was exhausted and he returned.”** On the retreat he defeated Wang Shuang.
   - In 231, Zhuge Liang again went out to Qishan and used “wooden oxen” for transport. Chen Shou says: **“Food was exhausted, he withdrew the army,”** and then he fought Zhang He and killed him.  
   Pei Songzhi’s annotation from *Han Jin Chun Qiu* even records a Shu victory over Sima Yi’s forces in this campaign, but the main text still says the retreat was caused by lack of food. That is the key point: a front victory did not solve the supply problem.
   - In 234, at Wuzhang Plains, Chen Shou says Zhuge Liang **“constantly worried that food would not continue, so that his ambition could not be fulfilled.”** He therefore divided troops to farm locally as a basis for long occupation. But he died before this could work.

2. **The mountain logistics made staying power extremely hard.**  
   Yi Province’s core was the Sichuan basin. The forward base was Hanzhong, and from Hanzhong the army had to cross the Qinling passes into Guanzhong. Narrow roads, porters, animals, and carts all consumed food on the way. The *Sanguozhi* mentions “wooden oxen and flowing horses,” but these were aids, not a solution. The sources do not give reliable tonnage figures, so I will not invent numbers. The repeated phrase **“liang jin”** — food exhausted — is the reliable evidence.

3. **Wei could trade space for time and reinforce.**  
   Wei could send Cao Zhen, Zhang He, Sima Yi, and others into the theater. Guanzhong and the Central Plains were closer to Wei’s core than Yi was to the front. Sima Yi’s strategy in 231 and 234 was essentially to avoid a decisive battle and let Shu-Han’s food run out. A Shu victory over a detachment did not destroy Wei’s main army or Wei’s ability to counterattack. So Shu-Han could win a battle and still be unable to hold the ground.

4. **Later Jiang Wei shows the same pattern.**  
   In 255, Jiang Wei won a major victory over Wei’s Yongzhou inspector Wang Jing at Taoxi, but he could not take Didao; when Wei relief forces came, he had to withdraw. Later he was badly defeated at Duangu. Again, a battlefield success did not translate into durable occupation.

5. **Romance vs. history.**  
   The phrase “six campaigns out of Qishan” is a *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* / folklore shorthand. In Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi*, Zhuge Liang’s northern campaigns are recorded as several operations, not all through Qishan, and the text repeatedly stresses **food exhaustion and withdrawal**. The novel often makes the victories more decisive and downplays the logistical collapse.

**Conclusion:** “Winning at the front” did not mean “holding the new territory” because holding required a continuous supply line, garrisons, local consolidation, and the ability to outlast Wei’s counterattacks. Shu-Han’s Yi-based logistics across the mountains made that extremely difficult, while Wei could wait and reinforce. That is why the *Sanguozhi* so often records a Shu advance, a victory or local success, and then a retreat because the food was gone.

q: Identify the stratagem: Wang Yun used Diaochan to sow suspicion between Dong Zhuo and Lü Bu, and in the end had Dong Zhuo killed by Lü Bu's hand. What is this stratagem usually called?
reply:
In the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* tradition, this is usually called the **Chain Stratagem** — **连环计 (Liánhuán Jì)**. It is also commonly described as a classic example of the **Beauty Stratagem** — **美人计 (Měirén Jì)**, because Diaochan is the key tool.

**Basis:** The title of Chapter 8 of *Sanguo Yanyi* is “Wang Yun Cleverly Uses the Chain Stratagem; Dong Zhuo Creates a Disturbance at Fengyi Pavilion” (王司徒巧使连环计，董太师大闹凤仪亭). In the novel, Wang Yun first promises Diaochan to Lü Bu, then gives her to Dong Zhuo, using her to provoke jealousy and fear between them; finally Lü Bu kills Dong Zhuo.

**Historical note:** This is a *Romance* version. In Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi*, **Diaochan is not recorded**. Dong Zhuo’s biography says Lü Bu had a secret affair with one of Dong Zhuo’s maidservants and feared discovery; Dong Zhuo had also once thrown a hand-halberd at Lü Bu. Wang Yun then persuaded Lü Bu to join the plot to kill Dong Zhuo. The woman is unnamed in the extant *Sanguozhi* and Pei Songzhi’s commentary; the elaborate Diaochan “chain stratagem” is a later literary creation.

q: Borrowing Arrows with Straw Boats: what weather conditions did Zhuge Liang take advantage of when he borrowed the arrows, and why did those conditions help him carry out the plan?
reply:
**Conclusion:** In the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, Zhuge Liang took advantage of a **heavy fog / dense mist on the Yangtze River** (大雾). The fog hid his straw boats and tricked Cao Cao’s troops into shooting arrows at what they thought was an enemy attack. This famous “borrowing arrows with straw boats” episode is **not found in Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi***; the closest historical anecdote is about **Sun Quan**, not Zhuge Liang.

**Romance account:**  
In the novel, Zhou Yu demanded 100,000 arrows. Zhuge Liang promised to get them in three days. On the third night, a thick fog covered the river. He sent boats loaded with straw bundles toward Cao Cao’s camp, beating drums and shouting. Cao Cao could not see clearly in the fog, so he ordered his archers and crossbowmen to shoot. The arrows stuck in the straw. By dawn, Zhuge Liang’s boats were full of arrows, and he returned before the fog lifted.

**Why the fog helped:**  
- It **obscured visibility**, so Cao Cao’s men could not tell that the boats were few, lightly manned, and covered with straw.  
- It made Cao Cao fear an ambush, so he relied on **ranged shooting** instead of sending ships out to fight.  
- The arrows could be **collected safely** in the straw without close combat.  
- The fog covered both the **approach and the retreat**, letting Zhuge Liang escape before Cao Cao realized the trick.  

**Historical note:**  
Chen Shou’s *Sanguozhi* does not record Zhuge Liang borrowing arrows. Pei Songzhi’s annotation quotes the *Weilüe* about **Sun Quan** at Ruxu: Sun Quan came in a large ship to observe Cao Cao’s camp; Cao Cao ordered arrows shot, and the arrows stuck in one side of the ship, making it tilt. Sun Quan turned the ship so the other side also received arrows, balancing it, and then returned. In that version, there is **no straw-boat trick, no Zhuge Liang, and no fog mentioned**.

So: the weather condition in the *Romance* is **dense fog**; historically, the story is a Romance adaptation of an anecdote about Sun Quan. The east wind belongs to the later “borrowing the east wind” episode for the fire attack, not to the arrow-borrowing episode.

q: The chained ships: before the Battle of Red Cliffs, who advised Ts'ao Ts'ao to link his warships together with iron chains? Why did this arrangement magnify the damage done by the fire attack?
reply:
**Conclusion.**  
In *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, it was **Pang Tong (Pang Tong)** who advised Cao Cao (Ts’ao Ts’ao) to link his warships with iron chains.  
In the official *Sanguozhi*, however, **no one is recorded as giving Cao Cao this advice**. The “iron chain stratagem” is a Romance invention. The *Sanguozhi* only records that **Huang Gai** observed Cao Cao’s ships were “首尾相接” — connected bow-to-stern — and proposed a fire attack.

**Evidence from *Sanguozhi*.**  
In the *Wu Shu*, *Zhou Yu zhuan*, Huang Gai says:

> “今寇众我寡，难与持久。然观操军船舰首尾相接，可烧而走也。”  
> “Now the enemy is numerous and we are few; it is hard to hold out long. But I observe that Cao Cao’s ships are connected bow-to-stern; we can burn them and drive them off.”

The main text does **not** say “iron chains,” and it does **not** name Pang Tong or any adviser. In the *Wudi Ji* account of Cao Cao, the defeat is attributed to military disadvantage and a great epidemic:

> “公至赤壁，与备战，不利。于是大疫，吏士多死者，乃引军还。”  
> “The duke reached Red Cliffs and fought Liu Bei; it was unfavorable. Then there was a great epidemic, and many officers and soldiers died, so he led the army back.”

Pei Songzhi’s notes add details about the fire attack, but they do not supply a scene of Pang Tong advising Cao Cao to chain the ships.

**Why the linked ships magnified the fire damage.**  
According to the historical narrative, once Huang Gai’s fire ships reached Cao Cao’s fleet, a strong wind spread the flames quickly. Because the ships were “connected bow-to-stern,” they could not easily scatter or cast off. A fire that began on one vessel could spread along the line, and the flames also reached the shore camps. Many men were burned or drowned. The arrangement turned a localized fire attack into a fleet-wide disaster.

So: **Romance answer — Pang Tong. Historical answer — no recorded adviser; the linked-ship detail appears only as Huang Gai’s observation, and “iron chains” is not specified in the *Sanguozhi*.**

q: Changban: who rescued the infant A'dou at Changban Slope? And who stood on Changban Bridge and scared off Cao Cao's army with his shouts?
reply:
**Conclusion:** In the *Sanguozhi* account, **Zhao Yun (Zhao Zilong)** rescued Liu Bei’s infant son **Liu Shan (A Dou)** at Changban, and **Zhang Fei (Zhang Yide)** held the rear at the bridge and deterred Cao Cao’s pursuers. The dramatic “stood on Changban Bridge and shouted Cao Cao’s army away” is mainly the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* version; the official history is more restrained.

**Evidence from *Sanguozhi*:**

1. **Zhao Yun rescued A Dou.**  
   In the *Sanguozhi*, *Zhao Yun zhuan* says that when Liu Bei was pursued by Cao Cao at Changban in Dangyang, Liu Bei abandoned his wife and children and fled south. Zhao Yun personally carried the young child—namely the Later Ruler, Liu Shan—and protected Lady Gan, the Later Ruler’s mother. Both escaped the disaster.  
   So historically, **Zhao Yun** is the one who saved A Dou. The *Romance* adds details such as “seven in, seven out” and Lady Mi’s suicide at the well; these are not in the *Sanguozhi* text.

2. **Zhang Fei held the bridge.**  
   In the *Sanguozhi*, *Zhang Fei zhuan* says Liu Bei ordered Zhang Fei to lead twenty horsemen to hold the rear. Zhang Fei took position by the water, broke the bridge, glared and leveled his spear, and shouted: “I am Zhang Yide; come and fight to the death!” The enemy none dared approach, and so they escaped.  
   So historically, **Zhang Fei** is the one at the bridge. But the *Sanguozhi* does **not** say he shouted three times, killed Xiahou Jie by fright, or that Cao Cao himself was scared off. It says only that the enemy did not dare come near after his challenge.

**Romance vs. history:** The “Changban Bridge” scene with Zhang Fei’s earth-shaking shouts belongs to the novel. The *Sanguozhi* does not even name the bridge as “Changban Bridge”; it says Zhang Fei “relied on the water and broke the bridge.” The core historical facts are: **Zhao Yun saved A Dou and Lady Gan; Zhang Fei deterred the pursuers at the broken bridge.**

q: Huarong Trail: in the novel, why does Guan Yu let Cao Cao go at Huarong Trail? What conflict within his character does this episode bring out?
reply:
**Conclusion:** In *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, Guan Yu lets Cao Cao go at Huarong Trail because Cao Cao appeals to Guan Yu’s sense of gratitude and old kindness, and because Zhang Liao is among Cao Cao’s retreating officers. The episode dramatizes Guan Yu’s inner conflict between **loyalty/duty (zhong)** to Liu Bei and **personal righteousness/gratitude (yi)** toward Cao Cao. In official history, however, there is no record of Guan Yu intercepting or releasing Cao Cao at Huarong; Cao Cao did retreat through Huarong, but the Guan Yu episode is a novelistic invention.

**The novel’s version:**  
After Red Cliffs in 208 CE, Cao Cao retreats. Zhuge Liang predicts he will take Huarong Trail and sends Guan Yu to ambush him. Guan Yu had made a military pledge to kill Cao Cao. When Cao Cao arrives, his army is exhausted and helpless. Cao Cao pleads with Guan Yu, reminding him of past kindness: Cao Cao had treated Guan Yu well when Guan Yu was in his service, and had allowed him to leave and return to Liu Bei. Guan Yu says he already repaid that by killing Yan Liang and Wen Chou. Cao Cao then reminds him of other favors, and Zhang Liao’s presence also moves Guan Yu. Unable to kill a defeated enemy who once treated him well, Guan Yu turns his horse aside and lets Cao Cao pass. He then returns and offers to be punished for breaking his pledge; Liu Bei intercedes for him.

**The character conflict:**  
Guan Yu is portrayed in the novel as the paragon of **yi**—righteousness, honor, and gratitude. At Huarong, he is torn between two obligations:

- **Loyalty to Liu Bei and military duty:** Killing Cao Cao would greatly weaken Wei and help Liu Bei’s cause. Guan Yu had sworn to do it.
- **Personal righteousness and gratitude:** Cao Cao had shown him kindness, and Guan Yu cannot bring himself to kill a helpless, defeated man who once treated him well.

He chooses personal righteousness over military orders. This reveals both his nobility and his flaw: he is compassionate, honorable, and magnanimous, but also sentimental and willing to let personal feeling override political and military logic. In the novel, this foreshadows later problems caused by his pride and independent judgment. It makes him a tragic hero rather than a coldly calculating general.

**Official history vs. the novel:**  
*Sanguozhi* does not record Guan Yu at Huarong. Cao Cao’s biography says that after Red Cliffs he suffered a great plague and withdrew.
